app.simulatedModeBody: Configs are read from a sample directory, not a real host. Control commands run in simulation, and probe/metric values are synthetic — they exist to demonstrate the interface. To work against a real server, run with NKT_MODE=local.
app.readOnlyMode: Changes are disabled by the NKT_ALLOW_MUTATIONS=false setting — the interface is read-only.

about.title: About
about.hint: The hub's own version and update check against GitHub Releases — separate from managed hosts' versions on the "Hosts" page.
about.updatableFalse: Self-update isn't available: the hub isn't currently running as a systemd unit. If this is Docker/Kubernetes — pull the new image and recreate the container: docker compose pull && docker compose up -d. If the binary was just launched by hand (e.g. right after downloading it with curl) — install and start it as a systemd service instead: sudo make hub-install && sudo systemctl enable --now netknownsthat-hub.
about.confirmUpdate: Update the hub to version {{version}}? It will download the binary, verify its checksum, and restart itself — unavailable for a few seconds.
about.restarting: The hub is updating and restarting itself — this can take up to a minute. This page will reload automatically once it responds again.
about.vulnDBHint: The centralized trivy database the hub uses to scan OS packages on every managed host — no host needs to download its own copy anymore (~1GB). Container image scanning still runs on the host itself: it needs that host's own Docker/Podman.

login.subtitle: Network resource map, config auditing, and host service management.
login.adminPasswordNote: The admin password is printed to the server log on first startup.

common.confirmDelete: Delete the {{what}} {{name}}? This can't be undone.
common.mutationsDisabled: Actions unavailable: needs the admin role and mutations enabled.
common.adminMutationsOnly: Available only to the admin role with mutations enabled (AllowMutations).
common.requestTimeout: Request {{path}} did not answer within {{seconds}}s. That usually means a command on the host is stuck — df on an unresponsive network share, for instance.

ptyToolbar.idleCountdownTooltip: Time until the session auto-closes from inactivity — resets on any input or output
ptyToolbar.tmuxMouseHint: With the mouse on, the wheel scrolls tmux history and selection goes to tmux — hold Shift to select in the browser

packageInstall.title: Installing {{packageName}}
packageInstall.connectError: Could not connect to the install session.
packageInstall.failed: Installation failed{{code}}. See the output above for what went wrong.

passwordForm.sessionsEnd: Changing your password ends every session — you'll need to sign in again.
passwordForm.forgot: Forgot your password and can't sign in? On the host, run sudo nkt passwd — this sets a new admin password without touching accumulated history.

updateModal.title: Package update
updateModal.willOffer: About to offer an update for: {{names}}. Confirmation (Y/n) happens right in the window below, like a normal terminal.
updateModal.connectError: Could not connect to the update session.
updateModal.rescanned: Host rescanned — the package list is already up to date.
updateModal.failed: Update failed{{code}}. See the output above for what went wrong.

findings.title: Configuration issues
findings.hint: The result of matching nginx, haproxy, and docker configs against the host's actual listeners and firewall rules. Each entry has an explanation and a concrete action.

audit.title: Audit log
audit.hint: Every change to the host's state — a service restart, a config edit, a firewall rule — is logged with the user, the result, and the command output.

interfaces.noLinkTooltip: Administratively enabled, but no response from the link partner — an unplugged cable, a disabled switch port, or the peer isn't up
interfaces.guessTooltip: Guessed from the interface name — not verified, unlike the docker labels above
interfaces.title: Network interfaces
interfaces.hint: Everything actually on the host per ip addr: physical NICs, bridges, VLANs, tunnels, loopback. Which one is public isn't decided here — that's determined precisely per-socket on the Overview, Firewall, and Findings pages.

users.title: Accounts
users.hint: Who can sign in to the web interface, and with what role. Passwords are stored irreversibly (argon2id) — a forgotten password can only be reset by setting a new one, via sudo nkt passwd <username> on the host itself.
users.confirmDelete: Delete the account {{username}}? This can't be undone.
users.roleHint: viewer is read-only, admin is full host control

lxd.hint: LXD containers and virtual machines — one tool manages both instance types.
lxd.none: LXD not found, or there are no instances.
lxd.newInstanceHint: lxc launch — the image downloads automatically, the instance starts right away.

podman.hint: Containers on Podman, a separate engine from docker — the same operations: start, stop, delete.
podman.none: Podman not found, or there are no containers.
podman.newContainerHint: The image is pulled if needed, the container is created and started right away.

docker.hint: Matching what's declared in compose against what's actually running.
docker.confirmDeleteRunning: Container {{name}} is running. Stop and remove it? This cannot be undone.

virt.transientTooltip: Transient domain: not registered via virsh define, so it has no saved definition or autostart. Disappears from the list when stopped.
virt.forceDestroyTooltip: Immediate forced shutdown — like pulling the power cord
virt.confirmDeleteWithDisks: Delete the VM {{name}} together with its disks? Disk images will be permanently deleted.
virt.confirmDeleteDefinition: Delete the VM {{name}}'s definition? Disks stay in place.
virt.title: Virtual machines
virt.hint: libvirt/QEMU domains — managed via virsh. Created and edited through the XML definition.
virt.none: libvirt not found, or there are no domains.
virt.newVmHint: Both paths end the same way — reviewing and editing the XML before saving.
virt.createDiskFile: Create the disk file (qemu-img create) — without this the XML will reference a file that doesn't exist
virt.invalidName: The name may only contain Latin letters, digits, dots, hyphens, and underscores
virt.applyVirshDefine: Apply (virsh define) — without this the XML is saved, but the domain isn't registered

hosts.notPasswordEncrypted: This file doesn't look like a password-encrypted export
hosts.tunnelActiveTooltip: SSH is currently unreachable — the dashboard, terminal, and reinstall/update are running over the fallback channel
hosts.tunnelConnectedTooltip: Fallback channel is connected and ready, but not currently in use — SSH is working
hosts.tunnelDisconnectedTooltip: Fallback channel is enabled in settings, but the hub hasn't connected to the host yet
hosts.notificationDenied: The browser didn't grant notification permission.
hosts.confirmForeignInstall:
This host already has nkt installed, not by this hub: {{detail}}.

Continue anyway? The binary, systemd unit, and env will be overwritten, and the admin password synced to what the hub stores — if this is someone else's install, access with its current password will be lost.
hosts.confirmRemoveSudo:
Remove passwordless sudo from "{{user}}" on "{{name}}"?

The hub won't be able to push updates or change anything on the host that needs root, until access is granted again (or the SSH user becomes root).
hosts.confirmStopHost: Stop nkt on "{{name}}"? The host will become unreachable through the hub until you start it again.
hosts.confirmBulkStart: Start nkt on every host at once ({{count}})?
hosts.confirmBulkStop: Stop nkt on every host at once ({{count}})? They'll all become unreachable through the hub until you start them again.
hosts.confirmUpdateAll: Update nkt on {{count}} hosts that are behind the hub's version? This runs sequentially, one host at a time.
hosts.confirmImport: Import hosts from this file? Hosts are added alongside existing ones (the file doesn't replace or dedupe by name/address). Secrets in the file only decrypt if it was exported with this same hub's NKT_HUB_MASTER_KEY.
hosts.confirmRemoveHost: Remove the host "{{name}}" from the hub? nkt itself is not removed from it.
hosts.thisMachine: this machine — the hub scans itself, no SSH
hosts.title: Hosts
hosts.hint: Each host is a separate VPS running its own nkt: the hub pushes the binary over SSH, sets it up as a systemd service, and proxies requests to it — so the dashboard and controls look no different from a plain single-host nkt.
hosts.exportWithKeyTooltip: For moving to a new hub without manually copying NKT_HUB_MASTER_KEY — the file becomes self-sufficient to decrypt, so keep it as carefully as passwords
hosts.notifyTooltip: Notifies via the browser about a new critical/high problem, or lost contact with a host — while this tab stays open
hosts.noHosts: No hosts yet — add the first one below.
hosts.jobRunning: in progress — you can close this window, the install continues in the background.
hosts.publicKeyBody: Add this line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the host itself (for the user given when it was added), then click "install". The matching private half is stored only on the hub and never leaves it.
hosts.confirmExportUnencrypted:
Download WITHOUT encryption?

The export file is plain JSON carrying the hub's own encryption key plus SSH/admin secrets for every host — whoever has the file has them. Without a password, anyone who gets it reads everything directly.
hosts.exportWithKeyBody: This file carries the hub's own encryption key plus every host's SSH/admin secrets in the clear — anyone who gets it can decrypt everything. Strongly recommended to encrypt it with a password right now rather than keep it as-is. The password isn't stored anywhere — lose it and the file becomes useless.
hosts.encryptPasswordLabel: Password to encrypt the file (optional, but recommended)
hosts.encryptedFileBody: "{{fileName}}" is password-protected — enter it to decrypt and import the hosts.
hosts.secretKeyEditing: New private key (PEM) — leave empty to keep the current one
hosts.secretPasswordEditing: New password — leave empty to keep the current one
hosts.name: Name
hosts.generatedKeyHint: No need to paste a private key anywhere — the hub generates its own pair and shows the public half after saving, which needs to be added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the host.
hosts.generatedKeyHintReplace: This host's previous auth method will be replaced by the new key.
hosts.terminalEnabled: enable a web terminal on the host
hosts.terminalEnabledHint: A full root shell right in the browser (the "Terminal" section on the host itself) — off by default.
hosts.reinstallsOnChange: Changing this setting immediately reinstalls nkt on the host (if already installed) to apply it.
hosts.appliesOnFirstInstall: Applies on this host's first install.
hosts.tunnelEnabled: fallback channel for when SSH is unreachable
hosts.tunnelEnabledHint: The hub keeps a separate secured connection to the host (port 8078 by default — NKT_HUB_TUNNEL_PORT on the hub) so the dashboard, terminal, and reinstall/update keep working even if SSH stops responding to it. No need to configure the hub's own address — the hub dials in the same way it does over SSH, using the same host address. On by default for new hosts; doesn't replace SSH for the very first install (nothing to fall back to yet).
hosts.addHostHint: The hub will connect over SSH, detect the architecture, build or reuse a cached nkt binary, and install it as a systemd service
hosts.bootstrapHint: A one-time bootstrap before install: add the missing packages, create a user with passwordless sudo, install the hub key and switch to key login. Debian/Ubuntu-like systems only.
hosts.bootstrapUser: User instead of root (empty keeps the current one)
hosts.bootstrapDisablePasswordHint: Done only after key login has been verified on a fresh connection; if the key stops working after sshd reloads, the change reverts itself.
hosts.removeIntro: The host is removed from the hub. Optionally, what nkt left on the server can be removed too — nothing is removed by default.
hosts.removeIntroVM: The machine will be removed from the hub. Separately, it can be deleted on the host itself — with or without its disks.
hosts.purgeVM: Delete the machine on its host
hosts.purgeVMHint: The host it was created on powers it off and removes the domain definition. No access to the machine itself is needed.
hosts.purgeVMDisksHint: Disk files are deleted for good. Without this, the disks stay in /var/lib/libvirt/images and the machine can be defined again.
hosts.purgeVMOnly: The rest concerns nkt inside the machine — it is being deleted whole, so there is nothing left to clean there.
hosts.purgeServiceHint: systemctl disable --now, then removing the unit, /usr/local/bin/nkt and /etc/netknownsthat. The server returns to its pre-install state.
hosts.purgeDataHint: /var/lib/netknownsthat (database, config version history, image archives) and /var/log/netknownsthat. The edit history cannot be recovered afterwards.
hosts.purgeAccessHint: The /etc/sudoers.d rule and the hub's key line in authorized_keys — other keys are left alone.
hosts.purgeUserHint: userdel -r together with the home directory. If people used the account, their files go too.
hosts.purgeUserRoot: The hub connects as root — that account cannot be removed.
hosts.removeUnreachable: If the server does not answer, the record is removed anyway and the response says nothing was touched on the host.
hosts.purgeFailed: {{name}} was removed from the hub, but nothing was removed on the server itself: {{error}}
hosts.bootstrapUserKey: Your public key for this user
hosts.bootstrapUserKeyHint: Optional. The hub's key is always installed; this one lets you SSH in as the same user the terminal and tmux run as.
hosts.purgeRestorePasswordHint: Removes the file the bootstrap used to disable passwords in sshd, checks the config with sshd -t and reloads it without dropping sessions. Otherwise, once the hub key is gone, the host has no way in at all.
hosts.groupEmpty: The group is empty — drag hosts here.
hosts.confirmDeleteGroup: Delete the group "{{name}}"? Its hosts ({{count}} now) go back to Ungrouped.
hosts.applyProfileBody: Hosts are visited one at a time: each gets its own plan, and only what actually differs there is applied. A failure on the first host stops the rollout, so a wrong description does not reach the whole group. The work runs in the background — follow it in the Jobs section.
hosts.applyProfileStarted: Rollout started: {{count}} hosts, job #{{job}}. Follow it in the Jobs section.
hosts.newVMBody: The host itself creates the machine from a cloud image, and the hub puts its own key inside on first boot and adds it to the list — inside that host. A machine has no group of its own: it moves between groups together with the host it runs on. Installing nkt on it stays a separate step. The work runs in the background; follow it in Jobs.
hosts.newVMStarted: Creation of machine "{{name}}" started, job #{{job}}. Follow it in Jobs.
hosts.applyProfileNone: Create a profile first in the Profiles section on the hub machine — there is nothing to roll out yet.
hosts.newVMKeyOptional: Optional: the hub always installs its own key and logs in with it. This one is only needed if you want to reach the machine directly, bypassing the hub.
hosts.newVMInstall: Install nkt on the new machine right after creation
hosts.detectAddressHint: The machine has not got an address from DHCP yet. Installing before that is pointless — a handshake with 0.0.0.0 fails anyway.
hosts.detectAddressFound: Address of "{{name}}" detected: {{addr}}. nkt can be installed now.
hosts.detectAddressNone: The address of "{{name}}" could not be determined: {{reason}}

detectAddressReason.no-domain: there is no machine with this name on the host — creation may not have finished, check the job log
detectAddressReason.not-running: the machine is not running (state: {{state}}) — start it and try again
detectAddressReason.no-lease: the machine runs but has no address yet: it is either still booting, or sits on a network with no DHCP lease and no guest agent. Wait a minute or set the address yourself via «edit»
detectAddressReason.no-virsh: the host could not answer: libvirt is unavailable or virsh is not installed

hosts.newVMToolsMissing: Host «{{host}}» is missing the tools needed to create machines — the job installs them itself as its first step. That takes a minute; you can install them up front:
hosts.newVMWillUpdate: Host «{{host}}» runs an nkt older than the hub. Creating a machine relies on its API, so the job will update it first — that takes a few minutes.
hosts.vmStarted: Machine “{{name}}” is starting; the address is detected on its own once it is up.

confirmVM.shutdown: Shut down “{{name}}”? The guest gets a power-button signal.
confirmVM.destroy: Power off “{{name}}” forcibly? This is like pulling the plug: unsaved data inside is lost.

hosts.discoverHint: libvirt domains not yet in the hub's list. Selected ones are registered as this host's machines; a powered-off one gets its address after it starts.
hosts.discoverNone: Every machine on this host is already listed.
hosts.discoverAuthHint: With a password the hub can log in and install nkt right away. Without one a hub key is generated — put it into the machine by hand; it is shown in the machine row (“public key”).
hosts.discoverKeyHint: The hub key is not in the machines yet — open “public key” in the machine row and add it to authorized_keys.

events.title: Alerts
events.hint: What happened to the hosts while nobody was watching: a host stopped answering, answered again, picked up serious findings. The hub records these during its background poll, so the log does not depend on an open tab, and the host name and address in it are the ones from the moment of the event.
events.settingsTitle: What to record and what to notify about
events.settingsHint: A hub-wide setting, not per browser. “Record” puts the event in the log; “notify” pops it up in the host-list tab when notifications are enabled there.
events.collapseHint: An “answering again” no later than this many minutes after “not answering” is folded into one line, “was down for N min”. 0 — never collapse.

changes.title: What changed
changes.subtitle: since you last looked ({{when}}) — changes: {{count}}
changes.subtitleNoBase: since the previous state snapshot — changes: {{count}}
changes.truncated: Not every change is shown — there are too many. Press “mark as seen” to see only new ones from now on.

certs.title: TLS certificates
certs.hint: Reads the files referenced by nginx's ssl_certificate and haproxy's crt directives. Checks expiry, name coverage, key strength, whether autorenewal will actually fire, and — via a separate TLS connection to the socket — whether the file on disk matches what clients actually see.
certs.scheduleHint: Time to expiry on a shared one-year scale — the order in which certificates will stop working
certs.noCertsDirectives: No ssl_certificate directive found in any parsed config.
certs.thresholdsNote: Thresholds: {{warn}}d — warning, {{critical}}d — urgent. Let's Encrypt renews 30 days before expiry, so a shorter runway means autorenewal already didn't fire.
certs.confirmRenewDerived: This is a copy of the certificate from {{source}} — the original will be renewed, and this copy will be automatically rebuilt from the new certificate and key, then the service reloaded.
certs.jobRunning: In progress — you can close this window, the process continues on the host in the background.
certs.unattachedHint: Present in /etc/letsencrypt/live, but no parsed config references them — everything certbot certonly issued (by hand or via the form above) lands here until something connects it to a service
certs.unattachedFooter: For a certificate to show up in "Details" above — wire it into a service's config (the "Configs" page) or assemble a PEM for haproxy with the form below.
certs.specifyDomain: Enter at least one domain name
certs.confirmIssue:
Issue a certificate for {{domains}}?

certbot certonly --standalone needs port 80/443 free — nginx and haproxy will be briefly stopped and automatically started back up once it finishes.
certs.issueTitle: Issue a new Let's Encrypt certificate
certs.issueHint: For a domain that doesn't have a certificate yet — certbot certonly --standalone. Wildcard names aren't supported: standalone proves ownership of only one exact name at a time.
certs.combineTitle: Assemble a haproxy PEM from certbot
certs.combineHint: Takes an already-issued certbot certificate from /etc/letsencrypt/live and glues it to its key into one file — what haproxy's crt needs. Doesn't call certbot renew.
certs.combinedSnippet: {{lineage}}: PEM assembled, valid until {{date}}. It isn't wired into any service yet — paste the directive below into the right file via the "Configs" page.
certs.combinedFileSuffix: was written, valid until {{date}}. haproxy reloaded its config — nothing to paste.
certs.listUpdated: The certificate list is already up to date.
certs.selfSignedHint: For internal services, or as a stopgap until a trusted-CA certificate is ready — the browser will still show a warning
certs.selfSignedResult: Certificate for {{names}} created, valid until {{date}}. It isn't wired into any service yet — paste the directives below into the right file via the "Configs" page.
certs.certbotMissing: Issuing and renewing certificates needs certbot, and the host does not have it. Self-signed certificates and combining for haproxy work without it.
certs.snippetNoteHaproxy: haproxy reads the certificate and key from one file — {{path}}. “Assemble a haproxy PEM” below builds it; without that file the bind will not come up.
certs.snippetNoteCaddy: caddy can obtain certificates itself; an external one is for when several services share one certificate.

fw.confirmCriticalPort:
WARNING: port {{port}} is the standard SSH port.

{{action}} could cut off SSH access to this host. An already-open session usually won't drop right away, but the next connection attempt will fail. Recovering access would then only be possible through the hosting provider's console or physical access.

Continue anyway?
fw.ufwOffNote: ufw is currently off — the rule is saved, but has no effect until you enable it.
fw.selectOneOption: Pick at least one: apply now or save permanently.
fw.confirmQuickAllow: Allow {{port}}/{{protocol}} in ufw from any source?
fw.ufwDisabledNote: ufw is off — has no effect
fw.hint: The full set of iptables, ufw, and firewalld rules with counters. Rules only change through ufw/firewalld: editing iptables directly from the web interface is a sure way to lock yourself out of the server.
fw.notInstalled: {{label}} is not installed on this host.
fw.addFirewalldRuleHint: A port or service in a zone, logged
fw.ufwRulesHint: Numbers shift after every change, so deletion is checked against the exact text you see.
fw.allRulesHint: Counters come from iptables-save -c: a zero counter means the rule has never matched.
fw.socketsHint: ss output: what's actually listening on ports

topology.title: Resource map
topology.hint: Red for critical problems, yellow for warnings. Hover or click a node to see the whole route — from the external network to the backend and back — and its details.
topology.findingsHint: {{count}} findings on the map — click a node for details
topology.clickNodeHint: Click a node on the map for details.

configs.confirmRollback: Restore version #{{id}}? The file's current content will be replaced.
configs.diffCaption: Differences between version #{{id}} and the current file — what rolling back to it would restore.
configs.title: Configs
configs.hint: Files found while parsing configs. Before writing, content is checked by the service itself (nginx -t, haproxy -c, caddy validate, docker compose config); if the check fails, the file is automatically reverted. Every edit is saved to history.
configs.selectFileLeft: Select a file on the left.
configs.noValidation: Config validation isn't available for this service — the file was written without validation.
configs.versionHistoryHint: The first entry is created automatically before the first edit
configs.emptyHistory: No history yet — this file hasn't been edited through this interface.
configs.cloneBody: The content of {{path}} (including unsaved edits, if any) will be written under the new path — the original file is untouched.
configs.pathHint: The directory must belong to nginx, haproxy, caddy, or be a path from NKT_COMPOSE_FILES — otherwise the server rejects the write.
configs.newFileSubtitle: new file — doesn't exist on disk yet
configs.notCreated: The file wasn't created — fix the content and try again.
configs.sshGuardProbeOk: sshd accepts a new connection (port {{port}}, {{banner}}). The check repeats after saving, and the edit rolls back automatically if the daemon stops accepting connections.
configs.sshGuardProbeFail: sshd is not accepting a new connection right now (port {{port}}): {{error}}
configs.sshGuardForce: I have console access to this host — allow the edit
configs.notWritable: This file is read-only: its directory is not writable from the nkt unit, and the sandbox could not be bypassed. Changes cannot be saved until the directory is opened up for the unit.
configs.allowWriteConfirm: Open this file's directory for writing by the nkt service? The setting goes into a separate unit file, after which the service restarts — open terminals and log streams will drop.
configs.allowWriteRestarting: The directory is open and the service is restarting. The file becomes writable in a few seconds; reload the page if it does not respond right away.
configs.pathNoDotDot: ".." is not allowed in the path
configs.pathSameAsSource: That is the source file’s own path — pick another

charts.noData: No data for the selected period.

services.title: Services
services.manualOriginTooltip: Started from an interactive session (SSH), not a service — won't come back after a reboot
services.hint: Manages systemd units. Every action is logged with the user who did it.
services.rescanTooltip: The list below is a snapshot, refreshed every few minutes — this button rescans the host right now
services.notTerminated: Process {{pid}} did not exit after SIGTERM.
services.clickToInstall: not installed on the host — click to install
services.clickToStart: installed but not running — click to start
services.notTerminatedInline: Process {{pid}}{{process}} did not exit after SIGTERM.
services.otherServicesSubtitle: sockets not described in any parsed config — found: {{count}}{{manual}}
services.allDescribed: Everything listening on this host is described in a parsed config.
services.stateUnknown: State could not be read: systemctl did not answer. Usually that means the dbus system bus is unavailable — see the Terminal section.

terminal.detachTooltip: Open in a separate browser window — survives navigating to other pages
terminal.tmuxTooltip: A tmux session survives closing the tab — reconnecting resumes the same one
terminal.connectError: Couldn't connect. The terminal may be disabled on the server (NKT_TERMINAL_ENABLED) — or this could be a plain network error.
terminal.checkingDbus: Checking D-Bus availability on the host…
terminal.dbusMissing: D-Bus isn't working on the host — the terminal (if it even opened), package updates, and self-update over the fallback channel are limited by the systemd unit's sandbox: they can't write to system paths. Usually because dbus isn't installed or isn't running (some minimal images, e.g. Debian 11, don't install it by default).
terminal.confirmInstallDbus: Install dbus (apt-get install -y dbus) and start it on this host?
terminal.manualDbusInstall: Automatic install isn't available on this host — install it by hand: apt-get install -y dbus && systemctl enable --now dbus.
terminal.dbusOk: D-Bus is available on the host — the sandbox doesn't limit the terminal or updates.
terminal.confirmOpenTmux: Open a terminal in tmux on this host? This is full shell access as the user nkt runs as (or the host's SSH user, if set). The tmux session survives closing the tab — reconnect the same way. This action is logged.
terminal.confirmOpen: Open a terminal on this host? This is full shell access as the user nkt runs as — usually root, or the host's SSH user if set. This action is logged.
terminal.confirmInstallTmux: tmux isn't installed on this host. Install it (apt-get install -y tmux) and open a session?
terminal.title: Terminal
terminal.hint: An interactive shell on this host, right in the browser. Requires an explicit host opt-in (NKT_TERMINAL_ENABLED=true) — if the server didn't enable it, connecting will fail with the error below.
terminal.toggleZoom: zoom pane in/out to full screen
terminal.wheelScroll: mouse wheel — scroll history (requires tmux mouse on)
terminal.diagnosisTitle: The terminal did not open. What is in the way:
terminal.diagnosisHint: Run these on the host from a console or over SSH — not from this terminal, which is the broken one:
terminal.dbusInstallFailedHint: The automatic install goes through the very path that is broken, so install dbus by hand — from the host console or over SSH:

commonPackages.title: Quick install
commonPackages.descTmux: terminal multiplexer — sessions survive a dropped connection
commonPackages.descCurl: command-line HTTP(S) and other protocol requests
commonPackages.descSsh: SSH server — accept incoming SSH connections
commonPackages.descNcdu: disk usage analyzer, browsable by directory
commonPackages.descNetTools: ifconfig, netstat, route and other classic networking tools
commonPackages.descMtr: traceroute and ping combined — route diagnostics

packages.title: Packages
packages.hint: Update OS packages, quick-install everyday tools, search and install any apt package, browse and remove what's already installed.
packages.searchPlaceholder: Name or part of the description…
packages.searchTruncated: Showing the first 200 matches — narrow the query to see the rest.
packages.confirmRemove: Remove package {{name}}? Config files are left in place (no --purge).
packages.confirmUpdate: Run apt-get dist-upgrade on this host ({{count}} packages)? apt will add/remove dependent packages as needed — you'll need to confirm (Y/n) in the window that opens.
packages.matchLegend: Packages whose name matched the query come first (highlighted); below are those where it only appears in the description.

overview.rebootRequired: Host reboot required — an update (not necessarily started from here) has already been applied and is waiting for a restart, e.g. after a kernel update.
overview.sortedBySeverity: Sorted by severity. Full list on the "Findings" tab.
overview.noOutages24h: No outages recorded over the last 24h.
overview.dataSourcesHint: What could be read during the last scan

vulns.title: Vulnerabilities
vulns.hint: Known CVEs for installed OS packages (Debian/Ubuntu) and for the images of already-running Docker/Podman containers — checked against a fresh trivy database. LXD isn't supported yet — it has no OCI images in the usual sense, that needs a separate mechanism.
vulns.neverScanned: No scan has been run on this host yet. The first run may need to download trivy and the vulnerability database (about 1 GB) — this can take a few minutes.
vulns.noDpkgStatus: This host has no /var/lib/dpkg/status — package scanning is only supported on Debian/Ubuntu.
vulns.noChangeSinceLast: Nothing changed since the last scan.
vulns.changeSinceLast: Since the last scan: +{{newCount}} new, {{fixedCount}} fixed.
vulns.firstRunNote: The first run may need to download trivy and the vulnerability database (about 1 GB) — this can take a few minutes.

availability.title: Availability schedule

usage.title: Network resource usage
usage.hint: Firewall counters, container stats, and parsed nginx/haproxy access logs. Logs are parsed by their record timestamp, so the chart shows when the load actually happened, not when it was collected.
usage.simulated: Metrics are synthetic: the host snapshot is static, so counters are simulated against a daily load profile. On a real host these would be increments of iptables counters and docker stats.
usage.scheduleHint: Average load by hour of week: shows working hours, night windows, and weekends.
usage.confirmOpenBtop: Open btop on this host? This is full access to processes as whichever user nkt runs under — usually root, or the host's ssh user if one is set. The action is logged.

usage.btopDisabled: btop isn't available: the web terminal isn't enabled on this host (set NKT_TERMINAL_ENABLED=true).
usage.btopFixturesDisabled: btop isn't available in fixtures mode — it's a static demo snapshot, there's no live host underneath to open a session on.
usage.btopAptGetMissing: apt-get not found — automatic btop install is only supported on Debian/Ubuntu. Install btop by hand and reload the page.

osUsers.title: Host accounts
osUsers.hint: Operating-system users and their SSH keys. Not the web interface accounts from «Users» — this grants login to the server itself.
osUsers.addHint: Creates the account if it does not exist and appends the key to its authorized_keys — existing keys are left alone.
osUsers.nameRule: Lowercase letters, digits, dash and underscore; starts with a letter or underscore, up to 32 characters — the same rules useradd uses
osUsers.keyRule: An authorized_keys line is expected: "ssh-ed25519 AAAA… comment". Options such as command= are not accepted here

disks.title: Disks
disks.hint: Space by filesystem, devices and partitions, swap. "What takes space" measures one level of subdirectories on demand — walking a large tree is slow.
disks.usageHint: Sizes of one level of subdirectories, largest first. Clicking a directory goes one level deeper.
disks.swapHint: Forgotten or full swap explains both missing space and sudden slowness.
disks.devicesHint: Physical disks with their partitions — what the kernel sees, mounted or not.

files.title: Files
files.hint: Browse host directories: folders, uploads (whole folders too — by button or by dropping onto the table), archives, git clone. Only inside the allowed roots — you can't go above them; system directories are edited through Configs with validation and history.
files.confirmDeleteFile: Delete file {{name}}? This cannot be undone.
files.confirmDeleteDir: Delete folder {{name}} with everything inside? This cannot be undone.
files.confirmExtract: Extract {{name}} into {{dir}}? Files with the same names will be overwritten.
files.tokenHint: The token is sent to the host once and lives only in the job's memory — it is never stored or logged. GitHub and GitLab don't need a username.
files.keyHint: The host's public key. Add it to the repository as a deploy key (GitHub: Settings → Deploy keys; GitLab: Settings → Repository → Deploy keys) and clone via the SSH URL.
files.dropHint: Drop to upload files and folders here

hardware.hint: What machine this is: CPU, memory, batteries and temperatures. Read-only — nothing here changes anything.

hardware.sensorsHint: Warning and critical thresholds come from the sensor itself — they differ between CPU and disk.

sysSettings.hint: Hostname, time zone, clock synchronisation and NetworkManager — the settings you configure once and then look up in the docs.

sysSettings.autoUpgradesMissing: unattended-upgrades is not installed — security updates are not applied automatically.
sysSettings.hostnameRule: Letters, digits and dashes; must not start or end with a dash, up to 63 characters (RFC 1123)
sysSettings.localesHint: Default: {{current}} · generated: {{installed}}. A locale must be generated before it can be made the default — tick the ones you need and press “Generate”.

sysSettings.ntpServersPlaceholder: pick from the list or type your own

errorBoundary.title: This section failed to render
errorBoundary.hint: This is a UI error, not a server one: other sections keep working. A report has been sent to the host's log — see the Logs section.

jobs.title: Jobs
jobs.hint: Long-running work happens in the background and does not depend on the browser: close the tab, lose the network — the job keeps going and its log is kept. Work interrupted by a service restart resumes from where it stopped wherever that is safe.
jobs.confirmCancel: Cancel the job "{{title}}"? What is already done is not rolled back.
jobs.interruptedHint: The job was interrupted by a service restart. What was already done is left as is — run it again when you are ready.

profiles.title: Profiles
profiles.hint: A profile describes what the host should be: packages, services, config files, open ports, accounts. The Plan button shows how reality differs and changes nothing; only ticked items are applied. A profile is additive — whatever it does not mention is left alone, never removed.

guide.title: How a profile works
guide.intro: A profile is a YAML description of a host's desired state: which packages must be installed, which services must run, what belongs in config files, which ports are open, who has access, and which compose stacks are up. It is not a programming language — no execution order, no conditions, no variables: just a flat list of what must be true.
guide.additive: A profile is additive and never turns off what it does not mention: a package missing from the list is not removed, an unmentioned service is not stopped. So "not specified" and "must be off" are different things — for services that is the difference between leaving the key out and writing "active: false".
guide.flow: The flow is: edit the description and save it, press "plan" — the host compares the description with reality and lists the differences one by one; untick anything you do not want applied and press "apply" — each item runs as a background job with its own log. A saved profile is then checked on its own, and drifted state shows up among the host's findings.

head.title: Header: version and name
head.body: version is the format version (1 today); name is the profile's name, shown in the list and in the job log.

packages.title: packages — packages
packages.body: Packages that must be installed; installed with apt. Extra ones are never removed — a profile only adds.

services.title: services — systemd units
services.body: Each unit has two independent flags: enabled (starts at boot) and active (running right now). Specify only what matters to you: a missing key means "none of my business", false means "must be off".

files.title: files — config files
files.body: The full content, not a hash: a hash shows a difference but gives nothing to fix it with. Writing goes through the same path as a manual edit: the content is validated by the service itself (nginx -t, docker compose config, …), recorded in the version history, and rolled back if validation fails. mode is octal; without it a new file is created 0644 and an existing file keeps its permissions.

firewall.title: firewall — open ports
firewall.body: Lists the ports that must be reachable. The profile does not decide whether the host uses ufw or firewalld — the host does. proto defaults to tcp; from narrows the source to an address or subnet. A rule for port 22 is flagged as risky: it can cut off your own access.

users.title: users — accounts
users.body: The account is created if missing; sudo: true grants passwordless sudo; keys are added to authorized_keys. Other keys are never removed — a person may have put them there, not a forgotten profile. Granting sudo and touching keys are flagged as risky.

system.title: system — hostname and timezone
system.body: The hostname shows up in certificates, logs and the shell prompt, so changing it is flagged as risky. timezone is a tzdata zone name.

compose.title: compose — services from docker compose
compose.body: A stack is described in full: name is the stack name (also the directory name and the docker project name), content is the compose file itself, up says whether the stack must be running (yes by default). Without an explicit path the file goes to /srv/compose/<name>/docker-compose.yml — its own directory, so applying a profile never overwrites what you maintain by hand. The plan shows two separate items — write the file and bring the stack up — so it is visible when running containers get recreated. up: false runs docker compose down; volumes are left alone. If the host has no docker, the plan offers to install it as its first item — the official way, from docker.com's repository: the distro package lags behind and may ship no compose plugin at all. It is a separate item and can be unticked.

limits.title: What a profile does not do
limits.packages: It never removes packages, services, files or accounts that the description does not mention.
limits.files: It does not watch a file after applying: the next check simply reports the difference.
limits.order: It expresses no ordering or dependencies — plan items run top to bottom, as shown.
limits.volumes: It never deletes data: docker compose down keeps volumes, and removing a disk or a directory stays a separate, manual step.

profiles.confirmDelete: Delete the profile "{{name}}"? Its edit history goes with it.

profiles.confirmApply: Apply the ticked items ({{count}})? The work runs in the background and does not depend on the browser.

profiles.saveBeforeApply: Save the profile first — what gets applied is the saved description, not the draft.

vmimages.title: VM images
vmimages.hint: Debian and Ubuntu cloud images: the system is already installed, and cloud-init creates a user with your key on first boot and grows the filesystem to the disk size. Downloads run in the background, survive a closed tab and resume where they stopped.
vmimages.confirmDelete: Delete the downloaded image "{{name}}"? VMs already created from it are unaffected — each has its own disk.
vmimages.name: Machine name
vmimages.templatesHint: A named hardware set: vCPUs, memory, disk, image and your key. The machine name is not part of a template — each machine has its own.
vmimages.templatesEmpty: No templates yet. Fill in the creation form and save it as a template.
vmimages.confirmDeleteTemplate: Delete the template "{{name}}"? Machines already created are unaffected.
vmimages.keyWillBeGenerated: No key given — nkt will create one: the public half goes into the machine, the private half is shown once after the start. Paste your own key below to use it instead.
vmimages.keyTitle: Private key of the new machine
vmimages.keyOnce: This key is shown once and stored nowhere. Copy it now — otherwise there will be no way into the machine except the virsh console.
vmimages.toolsMissing: This host is missing the tools needed to create machines. Creation installs them itself as its first step, but you can do it up front:

toolWhy.qemu-img: builds the machine disk from the image
toolWhy.genisoimage: the same, when cloud-localds is absent

vmimages.byURLHint: Fetched by the same job as catalog images, resuming after a break. The checksum is optional — without it the image is taken as is, unverified.
vmimages.byFileHint: Accepts .qcow2, .img and .raw. The file travels through the browser and the hub, so for a several-hundred-megabyte image a link is usually faster.
vmimages.hostHint: The libvirt disk directory (/var/lib/libvirt/images): both images placed there by hand and disks of existing machines.
vmimages.hostBusy: This is the disk of machine "{{vm}}". A copy will be made; the disk itself is untouched.
vmimages.hostBusyRunning: This is the disk of the running machine "{{vm}}". The copy is taken on the fly: the filesystem inside may end up inconsistent, as after a sudden power-off.
vmimages.hostEmpty: The libvirt disk directory is empty. Add your own image with the button on the right — by link or as a file from your computer.
vmimages.addOwnBody: The image goes into the libvirt disk directory (/var/lib/libvirt/images) — the same place machine disks live, and it shows up in the list below.
vmimages.confirmDeleteHost: Delete the file "{{name}}" from the libvirt disk directory? This cannot be undone.
vmimages.confirmDeleteHostBusy: The file "{{name}}" is the disk of machine "{{vm}}". Delete it? The machine will be left without a disk and stop starting.
vmimages.networkWillCreate: default — will be created on start

vmnet.title: VM networks
vmnet.hint: libvirt networks the virtual machines attach to. Not the server's own interfaces: this is where its machines look. Without such a network a machine does not start at all.
vmnet.confirmStop: Stop network "{{name}}"? Machines attached to it lose connectivity.
vmnet.confirmDelete: Delete network "{{name}}"? Machines attached to it will not start until another one is chosen.
vmnet.empty: This host has no libvirt networks — a machine would have nowhere to attach. Create one with the button on the right.
vmnet.name: Network name
vmnet.subnetHint: The host takes the first address, the rest go to the machines.
vmnet.force: Create anyway — overlapping the host's own network is intended
vmnet.autostartLabel: Bring up together with the host

mode.label: Kind
mode.nat: NAT: own subnet with outside access
mode.bridge: Bridge: machine on the host's network

modeHint.nat: This is how «default» works: machines get addresses from libvirt and reach out through the host. They are not visible from outside.
modeHint.bridge: The machine joins an already configured bridge and lives on the same network as the host: its own address from the shared DHCP, visible to neighbours.
modeHint.isolated: Machines see each other and the host, with no way out. Good for a test bench.

probe.title: Probe port {{port}}
probe.runHubHint: A connection from the hub itself, i.e. from outside: it shows whether the port is reachable through the firewall, not just whether the service answers inside the host
probe.curlHint: The line is split into arguments shell-style, but without a shell: quotes work, no substitutions or pipes. A -m timeout is added if you do not set one. Runs on the host.
probe.badJSON: The body is declared as JSON but does not parse as JSON.
probe.bannerHint: The banner — what the server sends on its own right after connecting (SSH, SMTP, FTP, Redis) — is always read; the reply to what you send is read until it goes quiet.
probe.silent: The connection opened but the server sent nothing — it waits for you to speak first.

standalone.intro: certbot --standalone runs its own server on ports 80/443, so they must be free for the check. This is what holds them now and what will happen to it:
standalone.free: Ports 80/443 are free — nothing needs stopping.
standalone.serviceFate: Service {{unit}} will be stopped while certbot runs and started back right after.
standalone.processFate: stop while certbot runs and relaunch with the same command
standalone.processDetail: directory {{cwd}}, user {{user}}; the environment is carried over. Started from a terminal — after relaunch it runs in the background, output goes to the systemd journal.
standalone.processLeft: Without a relaunch the port stays taken and certbot cannot validate the domain: stop the process yourself before issuing.
standalone.containerFate: Container {{id}}: nkt does not stop it. Free the port yourself and retry.
standalone.unknownFate: Could not read what this process is — nkt leaves it alone. Free the port yourself and retry.
standalone.processCaveat: Stopping is SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s. After certbot, nkt waits up to 15 s for the process to take the port again; if it does not, the log says so and names the command to start it by hand.
